analysis.one_liner: Funds the entire Defense Department for a year: military pay, health care, weapons, operations, and Iraq war costs.
analysis.headline: Passed with near-unanimous votes — the House 399-19, the Senate 95-0 — and was signed into law on September 30, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the annual spending bill for the Defense Department for fiscal year 2004. It pays service members, funds TRICARE health coverage, buys aircraft, ships, missiles, and ammunition, and pays for operations including Iraq and Afghanistan. It also carries guardrails: it bars funding for a controversial domestic surveillance research program except a narrow foreign-intelligence tool, forbids spending on nuclear-armed missile interceptors, and requires credit checks before government charge cards are issued.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families, whose pay, health coverage, and base services are funded; defense contractors, who receive the procurement and research dollars; veterans and communities near installations, who get environmental cleanup and emergency-preparedness grants; and the public, which gains a privacy safeguard against the Terrorism Information Awareness program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members, defense contractors, base communities

how_it_helps.text: Funds military pay, allowances, and retirement contributions for active-duty, reserve, and National Guard personnel across all services [S7].

Provides $15.7 billion for the Defense Health Program, including $7.4 billion for TRICARE health coverage contracts, and bars TRICARE reimbursement for inpatient mental health care referred by a provider with an economic interest in the facility [S7].

Prohibits the use of funds to research, develop, or deploy nuclear-armed missile interceptors, and bars funding for the Terrorism Information Awareness program except a narrow counterterrorism foreign-intelligence tool requiring congressional limits [S2,S6].
Appropriates funds for environmental restoration at current and formerly used defense sites, and for chemical stockpile emergency preparedness payments to state and local governments [S7].
Funds aid to public schools with high concentrations of military dependents and exempts service members hospitalized with war-related injuries from subsistence charges [S6].
Rescinds $3.49 billion of unneeded Iraq Freedom Fund money from the 2003 emergency wartime supplemental [S6].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who fund the entire appropriation, including tens of billions in weapons procurement routed to defense contractors and up to $15 billion in contingent liability for defense export loan guarantees.

drawbacks.text: The bill commits future taxpayer exposure of up to $15 billion through loan guarantees supporting U.S. defense exports [S3].
Buy American requirements for steel plate and anchor chain, and a ban on building naval vessels in foreign shipyards, protect domestic suppliers but can raise procurement costs [S3,S7].
The House voted 424-0 to close portions of the conference committee that reconciled the House and Senate versions, limiting public visibility into the final negotiations [S12].

The bill assumes $1.66 billion in savings from outsourcing and management efficiencies and permits depot work to be competed against private firms, putting Defense Department civilian work under cost pressure even while restricting conversions that lack a competition showing at least 10 percent savings [S6,S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does the ordinary work of funding the military and adds real guardrails — the surveillance-program restriction, the nuclear-armed interceptor ban, a lobbying prohibition, and charge-card credit checks. The costs are the ordinary ones of a defense budget: tens of billions flow to a concentrated set of contractors under multiyear contracts, export loan guarantees shift financial risk onto taxpayers, and key negotiations happened partly behind closed doors. Nothing here is unusual for a defense appropriations bill, which is part of the point: the process was smooth and nearly unanimous.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by overwhelming margins, a conference committee merged the versions with parts of its negotiations closed to the public, both chambers agreed to the result, and the President signed it on September 30, 2003.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Appropriations reported the bill as an original measure on July 2, 2003, and the House passed it 399-19 on July 8, with 222 of 229 Republicans and 177 of 205 Democrats in favor [S10,S9].

The Senate amended the bill and passed it 95-0 on July 17, adding provisions including a near-total ban on the Terrorism Information Awareness research program and settlement payments to World War II prisoners of war forced into labor by Japanese companies [S11,S4].
On September 16 the House voted 424-0 to close portions of the conference committee negotiating the final version [S12].
The House agreed to the conference report 407-15 on September 24 and the Senate agreed 95-0 on September 25 [S13,S14].
The President signed it on September 30, 2003, and it became Public Law 108-87 [S6,S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Pentagon and its contractors received their full fiscal 2004 funding with almost no friction; service members got funded pay and health coverage; and privacy advocates won a notable restriction that cut off funding for the Terrorism Information Awareness program except a narrow foreign-intelligence tool.

sides.party_line_note: This was not a partisan fight: the House passed it 399-19 with about 96% of Republicans and 86% of Democrats in favor, the Senate passed it twice at 95-0, and only 19 House members and 15 House members opposed it on the two final votes.

industries.industry: Defense contractors (aircraft, missile, ship, and ammunition makers)
industries.note: The bill routes tens of billions in procurement and research dollars to defense contractors and authorizes multiyear contracts for F/A-18 and E-2C aircraft, the Tactical Tomahawk missile, and a Virginia-class submarine [S6]. Buy American requirements and a ban on building naval vessels in foreign shipyards lock domestic suppliers into that revenue stream [S3,S7]. Their gain is paid for by taxpayers, though the same spending funds national security and military payrolls.

industries.industry: TRICARE health care contractors and providers
industries.note: The bill provides $7.4 billion for TRICARE contracts, keeping private contractors as the channel for military family health coverage, while adding a guardrail barring reimbursement for mental health care referred by providers with a financial stake in the facility [S7].

industries.industry: Defense consultants and federally funded research centers
industries.note: The bill cuts $74.2 million from FFRDC funding, caps their staffing, bans creating new ones, and trims $504.5 million from advisory and assistance services growth [S6].

industries.industry: Private contractors seeking outsourced Defense Department work
industries.note: The bill assumes $1.66 billion in savings from outsourcing and allows depot work to be competed with private firms, but bars converting any function performed by more than 10 civilian employees to contractors without a public-private competition showing at least 10 percent savings [S6,S7].
